title: Getting started
summary: Rust is a systems language that aims for speed and memory safety without a garbage collector. You write crates, build them with Cargo, and start binaries at fn main.
bullets: Install the toolchain with rustup, then use cargo new, cargo build, and cargo run.
A crate is a compilation unit. A binary crate needs fn main.
The compiler (rustc) checks types, ownership, and borrows before your program runs.
Comments start with // or /* */.

title: Variables and types
summary: Bindings are immutable unless you write mut. Common types include i32, u32, f64, bool, char, String, and &str.
bullets: let x = 5; cannot be assigned again. let mut x = 5; can.
Shadowing (another let with the same name) can even change the type.
Integer overflow panics in debug builds and wraps in release by default.
char is a Unicode scalar value. String is owned UTF-8. &str is a borrowed slice.

title: Ownership and borrowing
summary: Each value has one owner. Assigning a String moves it. Borrowing with & or &mut lets you use a value without taking it.
bullets: Moves transfer ownership. The old name cannot be used.
Copy types (integers, bool, char) are duplicated instead of moved.
You may have many shared &T borrows, or one exclusive &mut T, not both at once.
Slices (&[T], &str) are borrowed views into existing data.

title: Control flow
summary: if and match are expressions. loop, while, and for repeat work. Ranges use .. (exclusive) and ..= (inclusive).
bullets: Both arms of an if used as a value must have the same type.
match is exhaustive: every variant must be handled or covered by _.
for n in 1..5 walks 1, 2, 3, 4.
loop is infinite until you break (and break can yield a value).

title: Structs, enums, and match
summary: Structs group fields. Enums name a set of variants that can carry data. impl adds methods. Option and Result are enums you will use constantly.
bullets: Methods take self, &self, or &mut self.
Option<T> is Some(T) or None. Result<T, E> is Ok(T) or Err(E).
Prefer match or ? over unwrap in real code.
#[derive(Debug)] generates a Debug impl so you can print with {:?}

title: Collections
summary: Vec, String, and HashMap cover most day-one data work. Iterators let you map, filter, and collect without writing every loop by hand.
bullets: vec![1, 2, 3] builds a Vec. len, push, iter, and collect are the usual tools.
String is growable; push_str appends a &str.
HashMap::get returns Option<&V>.
Iterator adapters are lazy until a consumer like sum or collect runs.
examples:
let nums = vec![1, 2, 3];
let doubled: Vec<i32> = nums.iter().map(|n| n * 2).collect();

title: Error handling
summary: Use Result for recoverable failures. ? returns the Err to the caller or continues with the Ok value. Panic is for bugs, not expected I/O errors.
bullets: parse, File::open, and many std APIs return Result.
? needs a function that can return that error type.
ok_or converts Option into Result.
Custom error enums keep failure modes readable.

title: Traits and generics
summary: Generics write one function for many types. Trait bounds say what those types must be able to do. Lifetimes are names the compiler uses to check borrows.
bullets: fn larger<T: PartialOrd>(a: T, b: T) -> T is generic over comparable types.
impl Trait for Type supplies the trait's methods.
A lifetime 'a on a returned &str ties it to the inputs.
The apostrophe in 'a is a lifetime, not a character literal.

title: Next steps
summary: After you can read ownership, Result, and traits, the Rust Book chapters on testing, Cargo, and modules will feel much easier.
bullets: Work through the Rust Book and Rust by Example.
rustlings is a set of small local exercises.
cargo test, rustfmt, and clippy are the daily tools.
Come back here and type the intermediate and advanced snippets.
